      <div><p class="kick">BIM insights</p><h2>Notes from the <em>model.</em></h2></div>
      <p class="lead">Short guides for owners, architects and contractors who want to get more from BIM on their next project.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="igrid">
      <details class="art">
        <summary><span class="ak">Guide · 3 min read</span><h3>LOD 100 to 500: how much detail does your project need?</h3><p>Level of Development tells everyone how far a model element can be trusted. Choosing it well saves time and money.</p><span class="more">Read article</span></summary>
        <div class="abody">
          <p>LOD describes how developed, and how reliable, each element in a BIM model is. It is agreed at the start of a project, usually in the BIM Execution Plan, so every team knows what they can rely on.</p>
          <ul><li><b>LOD 100:</b> massing only. Good for early feasibility, site planning and area studies.</li><li><b>LOD 200:</b> generic elements with approximate size and position. Used during design development.</li><li><b>LOD 300:</b> exact sizes and locations. Ready for general arrangement drawings and quantities.</li><li><b>LOD 350:</b> adds the interfaces between systems, such as where ducts pass beams. The level for coordination and clash detection.</li><li><b>LOD 400:</b> fabrication detail: plates, bolts and connections. Used for shop drawings in steel, precast, facade and MEP.</li><li><b>LOD 500:</b> verified against what was built. The as-built record for the owner.</li></ul>
          <p>The rule of thumb: model each element only to the level the next decision needs. Over-modelling early wastes budget; under-modelling late causes problems on site.</p>
        </div>
      </details>
      <details class="art">
        <summary><span class="ak">Explainer · 3 min read</span><h3>Scan to BIM: turning an existing building into a model</h3><p>Renovating or extending an older building? A laser scan and a Revit model replace guesswork with measured fact.</p><span class="more">Read article</span></summary>
        <div class="abody">
          <p>Many existing buildings have no reliable drawings. Scan to BIM fixes that in three steps.</p>
          <ul><li><b>Scan:</b> a laser scanner captures millions of measured points, the point cloud, inside and outside the building.</li><li><b>Model:</b> the point cloud is brought into Revit and traced into real walls, floors, roofs, openings and structure.</li><li><b>Use:</b> the model becomes the base for renovation design, quantities, MEP upgrades and an accurate as-built record.</li></ul>
          <p>It is most useful for heritage buildings, retrofits, extensions and facilities that need an asset record. Agree the level of detail and accuracy before modelling starts, so the model fits its purpose.</p>
        </div>
      </details>
      <details class="art">
        <summary><span class="ak">For homeowners · 2 min read</span><h3>Why your villa should be modelled before it is built</h3><p>A 3D model of your home catches clashes, fixes costs and lets you walk every room before construction begins.</p><span class="more">Read article</span></summary>
        <div class="abody">
          <p>For a villa, BIM is not only for large projects. A coordinated model helps owners, designers and builders in practical ways.</p>
          <ul><li><b>See it first:</b> 3D views and cutaways show every room, light and finish before money is spent.</li><li><b>Fewer site surprises:</b> beams, ducts, plumbing and ceilings are checked against each other in the model, not on site.</li><li><b>Clear quantities:</b> walls, floors and finishes can be measured from the model for more reliable estimates.</li><li><b>Better drawings:</b> plans, sections and joinery details all come from one model, so they agree with each other.</li></ul>
          <p>The result is a smoother build, fewer changes and a home that matches the design.</p>
        </div>
      </details>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>
